steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Overview
  - user mode = system-defined processes and DLLs
  - "environment subsystem" = interface between user mode apps and kernel functions
  - NT can have several, each a different API set; meant to support apps written for many OS types
  - no direct hardware access; call into kernel mode routines
  - three main ones: Win32, OS/2, POSIX
### Win32 environment subsystem
- runs 32-bit Windows apps
- console, text window support, shutdown, hard-error handling for all other subsystems
- Virtual DOS Machines (VDMs): MS-DOS and 16-bit Windows (Win16) apps
- MS-DOS VDM: own address space, emulates Intel 80486 running MS-DOS 5.0
- Win16 VDM: programs by default in same process/address space, each gets own thread
- option: separate Win16 VDM per program -> preemptive multitasking (NT pre-empts whole VDM process)
- csrss.exe also has window management ("window manager"): handles keyboard/mouse input, passes messages to apps
- apps draw/refresh own windows and menus in response
### OS/2 environment subsystem
- 16-bit character-based OS/2 apps, emulates OS/2 1.x; not 32-bit or graphical (OS/2 2.x+); x86 only
- graphical OS/2 1.x needs Windows NT Add-On Subsystem for Presentation Manager
- last in Windows 2000; discontinued as of Windows XP
### POSIX environment subsystem
- apps strictly written to POSIX.1 or related ISO/IEC standards
- replaced by Interix (part of Windows Services for UNIX), then by Windows Subsystem for Linux
### Security subsystem
- [quote: what the security subsystem manages]
- security system process = Local Security Authority (LSA): security tokens, grants/denies access [quote: user accounts, login, auditing]
- also looks after Active Directory
- workstation service: network redirector, client side of file/print sharing, redirects requests to servers
- server service: lets other computers access local file shares and shared printers

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
User mode consists of various processes and DLLs that are defined by the system.

An "environment subsystem" is the interface between user mode applications and the functions of the operating system kernel. Windows NT can have more than one environment subsystem, and each one implements a different API set. The idea of this mechanism was to support applications that were written for many different types of operating systems. None of the environment subsystems can access hardware directly; to access hardware functions they call into kernel mode routines.

The three main environment subsystems are the Win32 subsystem, an OS/2 subsystem and a POSIX subsystem.

### Win32 environment subsystem

The Win32 environment subsystem can run 32-bit Windows applications. It contains the console and text window support, and it also does shutdown and hard-error handling for all the other environment subsystems. It supports Virtual DOS Machines (VDMs) too, which let MS-DOS and 16-bit Windows (Win16) applications run on Windows NT. There is a specific MS-DOS VDM which runs in its own address space and emulates an Intel 80486 running MS-DOS 5.0. Win16 programs run in a Win16 VDM instead. By default each program runs in the same process, so they use the same address space, and the Win16 VDM gives each program its own thread to run on. But Windows NT does let users run a Win16 program in a separate Win16 VDM. This allows the program to be preemptively multitasked, because Windows NT will pre-empt the whole VDM process, and that process only contains one running application. The Win32 environment subsystem process (csrss.exe) also includes the window management functionality, which is sometimes called a "window manager". It handles input events, such as from the keyboard and mouse, and then passes messages to the applications that need to get this input. Each application is responsible for drawing or refreshing its own windows and menus when it gets these messages.

### OS/2 environment subsystem
- 16-bit character-based OS/2 apps, emulates OS/2 1.x; not 32-bit or graphical (OS/2 2.x+); x86 only
- graphical OS/2 1.x needs Windows NT Add-On Subsystem for Presentation Manager
- last in Windows 2000; discontinued as of Windows XP

### POSIX environment subsystem
- apps strictly written to POSIX.1 or related ISO/IEC standards
- replaced by Interix (part of Windows Services for UNIX), then by Windows Subsystem for Linux

### Security subsystem
- "manages operating system-specific functions on behalf of the environment system and consists of a security system process"
- security system process = Local Security Authority (LSA): security tokens, grants/denies access "to user accounts based on resource permissions, handles login requests and initiates login authentication, and determines which system resources need to be audit[ed]"
- also looks after Active Directory
- workstation service = network redirector, client side of file/print sharing
- server service: other computers access local file shares and printers

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
User mode consists of various processes and DLLs that are defined by the system.

An "environment subsystem" is the interface between user mode applications and the functions of the operating system kernel. Windows NT can have more than one environment subsystem, and each one implements a different API set. The idea of this mechanism was to support applications that were written for many different types of operating systems. None of the environment subsystems can access hardware directly; to access hardware functions they call into kernel mode routines.

The three main environment subsystems are the Win32 subsystem, an OS/2 subsystem and a POSIX subsystem.

### Win32 environment subsystem

The Win32 environment subsystem can run 32-bit Windows applications. It contains the console and text window support, and it also does shutdown and hard-error handling for all the other environment subsystems. It supports Virtual DOS Machines (VDMs) too, which let MS-DOS and 16-bit Windows (Win16) applications run on Windows NT. There is a specific MS-DOS VDM which runs in its own address space and emulates an Intel 80486 running MS-DOS 5.0. Win16 programs run in a Win16 VDM instead. By default each program runs in the same process, so they use the same address space, and the Win16 VDM gives each program its own thread to run on. But Windows NT does let users run a Win16 program in a separate Win16 VDM. This allows the program to be preemptively multitasked, because Windows NT will pre-empt the whole VDM process, and that process only contains one running application. The Win32 environment subsystem process (csrss.exe) also includes the window management functionality, which is sometimes called a "window manager". It handles input events, such as from the keyboard and mouse, and then passes messages to the applications that need to get this input. Each application is responsible for drawing or refreshing its own windows and menus when it gets these messages.

### OS/2 environment subsystem

The OS/2 environment subsystem supports 16-bit character-based OS/2 applications and emulates OS/2 1.x. It does not support 32-bit or graphical OS/2 applications like the ones used with OS/2 2.x or later, and it only works on x86 machines. The Windows NT Add-On Subsystem for Presentation Manager has to be installed to run graphical OS/2 1.x programs. Windows 2000 was the last version of Windows NT that had an OS/2 subsystem; it was discontinued as of Windows XP.

### POSIX environment subsystem

The POSIX environment subsystem supports applications written strictly to either the POSIX.1 standard or the related ISO/IEC standards. This subsystem was replaced by Interix, which is part of Windows Services for UNIX. Interix was then replaced by the Windows Subsystem for Linux.

### Security subsystem

The security subsystem "manages operating system-specific functions on behalf of the environment system and consists of a security system process". This security system process is the Local Security Authority (LSA). The LSA manages security tokens and grants or denies access "to user accounts based on resource permissions, handles login requests and initiates login authentication, and determines which system resources need to be audit[ed]" by Windows NT. It also looks after Active Directory. The workstation service implements the network redirector, which is the client side of Windows file and print sharing. It implements local requests to remote files and printers by "redirecting" them to the right servers on the network. The other way around, the server service lets other computers on the network access the file shares and shared printers that the local system offers.

steps.text:
User mode is made up of various system-defined processes and DLLs.

The interface between user mode applications and operating system kernel functions is called an "environment subsystem". Windows NT can have more than one of these, each implementing a different API set. This mechanism was designed to support applications written for many different types of operating systems. None of the environment subsystems can access hardware directly; hardware functions are accessed by calling into kernel mode routines.

There are three main environment subsystems: the Win32 subsystem, an OS/2 subsystem and a POSIX subsystem.[1]

### Win32 environment subsystem

The Win32 environment subsystem can run 32-bit Windows applications. It contains the console as well as text window support, shutdown and hard-error handling for all other environment subsystems. It also supports Virtual DOS Machines (VDMs), which allow MS-DOS and 16-bit Windows (Win16) applications to run on Windows NT. There is a specific MS-DOS VDM that runs in its own address space and emulates an Intel 80486 running MS-DOS 5.0. Win16 programs, however, run in a Win16 VDM. By default each program runs in the same process, thus using the same address space, and the Win16 VDM gives each program its own thread to run on. However, Windows NT does allow users to run a Win16 program in a separate Win16 VDM, which allows the program to be preemptively multitasked, since Windows NT will pre-empt the whole VDM process, which only contains one running application. The Win32 environment subsystem process (csrss.exe) also includes the window management functionality, sometimes called a "window manager". It handles input events (such as from the keyboard and mouse), then passes messages to the applications that need to receive this input. Each application is responsible for drawing or refreshing its own windows and menus in response to these messages.

### OS/2 environment subsystem

The OS/2 environment subsystem supports 16-bit character-based OS/2 applications and emulates OS/2 1.x, but not the 32-bit or graphical OS/2 applications used with OS/2 2.x or later, and only on x86 machines.[2] To run graphical OS/2 1.x programs, the Windows NT Add-On Subsystem for Presentation Manager must be installed.[2] The last version of Windows NT with an OS/2 subsystem was Windows 2000; it was discontinued as of Windows XP.[3,4]

### POSIX environment subsystem

The POSIX environment subsystem supports applications that are strictly written to either the POSIX.1 standard or the related ISO/IEC standards. This subsystem has been replaced by Interix, which is part of Windows Services for UNIX.[3] This was in turn replaced by the Windows Subsystem for Linux.

### Security subsystem

The security subsystem "manages operating system-specific functions on behalf of the environment system and consists of a security system process". This security system process is the Local Security Authority (LSA), which manages security tokens and grants or denies access "to user accounts based on resource permissions, handles login requests and initiates login authentication, and determines which system resources need to be audit[ed]" by Windows NT.[5] It also looks after Active Directory. The workstation service implements the network redirector, the client side of Windows file and print sharing; it implements local requests to remote files and printers by "redirecting" them to the appropriate servers on the network.[6] Conversely, the server service allows other computers on the network to access the file shares and shared printers offered by the local system.[7]
